title: Build or Buy AI Tools: Why Renting Capability Backfires
author: Gleb Tsipursky
summary: Behavioral scientist Gleb Tsipursky argues that the standard corporate approach to AI, buying a finished platform from a vendor, solves an immediate problem but fails to build durable organizational capability, because the vendor retains the practical knowledge to modify the tool while the company only owns the license. His alternative is to teach employees to help design, test, and improve their own AI tools within governed limits, on the premise that domain experts (the claims processor, the customer-service rep) understand which parts of their own workflow require judgment better than any outside developer, a claim he backs with a 5,179-agent customer-support study showing AI assistance produced 14 percent average productivity gains, concentrated most heavily among less-experienced workers. He lays out a graduated implementation path: start with a single recurring task employees already want automated, begin with visible expert-supported co-creation before shifting ownership to employees, and build a small cross-functional enablement group (business champions, IT, security, an executive sponsor) to maintain governance. Tsipursky is explicit that this employee-builder model has firm limits, professional developers should still own complex integrations, sensitive data systems, and high-stakes decisions like loan approvals or employment outcomes, and argues organizations should measure success less by hours saved than by what employees, managers, and IT collectively learn about testing, risk, and value through the process.
points: Tsipursky's central diagnosis of vendor-bought AI tools is a knowledge-asymmetry problem: 'the company owns licenses, yet the vendor owns the practical knowledge,' meaning every workflow adjustment requires another procurement cycle rather than an internal fix.

He grounds the domain-expert argument in a specific productivity study of 5,179 customer-support agents, where AI assistance produced a 14 percent average productivity gain concentrated most heavily among less-experienced workers, evidence that AI's biggest value comes from encoding expert practice, not from raw technology.

His implementation sequence is concrete and de-risked: start with one recurring task employees already want automated, run the first build with visible expert support ('build in the open'), then shift ownership to employees for subsequent tools, a graduated co-creation model rather than an all-at-once rollout.

He specifies enforceable guardrails rather than vague governance principles: approved platforms only, named ownership for every tool, adversarial testing before deployment, and mandatory human review for high-impact decisions.

He draws an explicit boundary for where employee building must stop, citing loan approval, medical recommendations, and employment decisions as examples of systems that require professional engineering and risk management regardless of how much domain expertise a citizen builder has.
quotes: The company owns licenses, yet the vendor owns the practical knowledge. That arrangement may deliver a tool. It rarely creates internal AI capability.
Buying an AI tool solves a defined problem at a specific moment. Building capability changes how the organization responds to problems for years.

The claims processor knows which parts of a file require judgment. The customer-service representative knows which questions waste the most time. The HR coordinator knows where onboarding repeatedly breaks down.
In a study of 5,179 customer-support agents, access to an AI assistant increased productivity by 14 percent on average, with much larger gains among less-experienced workers.
Citizen builders should not quietly construct systems that approve loans, make medical recommendations, determine employment outcomes, or bypass established controls.

Do not ask only, "Which AI system should we buy?" Ask, "What must our people learn to build, improve, and govern for themselves?" Vendors can supply technology. Consultants can accelerate the journey. Neither should own your organization's ability to innovate.
